items.title: US-China power gap narrows as Beijing gains ground, Lowy report finds
paras: US President Donald Trump has lost ground in Asia as Chinese President Xi Jinping gained influence. ( Reuters: Brendan Smialowski )
The latest Lowy Institute report found the US has lost ground in power and influence across Asia.
South-East Asia faces mounting geopolitical pressure, with diplomatic influence declining across the region.
India has strengthened its overall influence while Australia's comprehensive power has dipped slowly.
The United States has lost a significant amount of power and influence in Asia this year, research has shown, with China gaining ground.

The Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index found that the Trump administration's war with Iran and other unpopular policy decisions had contributed to a record decline in US diplomatic influence in Asia.
China, by contrast, held steady across most measures, while strengthening its military capability, cultural influence and resilience, adding to its overall power in the region.
China ranked first in the Index's measures of Economic Relationship and Diplomatic Influence, ahead of the US in both.
While Washington remains the dominant power in the region according to the index, the gap between the US and China's military capabilities is now at its narrowest point on record.
"This narrowing divide owes more to Washington's missteps than to any advances on Beijing's part," authors Hunter Marston and Jack Sato wrote.
"Respondents to the Asia Power Index survey saw the United States as distracted and disengaged in Asia."
Anthony Albanese was rated more effective at advancing Australia's economic interests than its diplomatic interests in Asia, the index found. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
Australia's comprehensive power score dipped slightly from last year , and it fell one place to sixth, behind Russia.
The report credited Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with advancing Australia's economic interests but rated him less effective at furthering diplomatic interests in Asia.
The index found the Trump administration’s diversion of resources away from the Pacific to the Middle East saw US leadership lose influence and power in the region. ( AP: Jacquelyn Martin )
The index found the Trump administration's diversion of resources away from the Pacific to the Middle East coincided with deeper defence ties among US treaty allies in the region.

"The United States' unresolved war with Iran has eroded US military capabilities by depleting its stockpile of long-range missiles, and profoundly undermined perceptions of US diplomatic influence both regionally and globally," the report said.

That, along with the US pressing countries to spend more on their own defence and calling for fewer joint military exercises with South Korea, left negative impressions of US leadership, the report said.
With the US recording declines in economic and military capabilities, the two superpowers — China and the US — are now almost tied in economic capability in the region.

"The gap between the two is now 5.3 points, the narrowest since the inception of the Index, but it's still a clear lead for the US," said Mr Sato, a data analyst and researcher on the Asia Power Index at the Lowy Institute.
He told the ABC that the narrowing comprehensive power scores reflected three factors.

"A series of missteps by a more transactional US", conflicts elsewhere "drawing US attention and its defence networks away from the Indo-Pacific", and China's fast military expansion decreasing the US lead in Military Capability "from 27 points in 2018 to just over 15".

It was a tough year for countries in the Asia-Pacific region, with the disruption of global energy supplies from the Middle East conflict and Strait of Hormuz closure hitting the region particularly hard.
Queues formed for fuel in the Philippines earlier this year as the government introduced measures to reduce fuel use. ( Reuters: Lisa Marie David )
Higher fuel and fertiliser prices constrained food and agricultural production, putting more political pressure on leaders.
As a result, government effectiveness declined across nearly all South-East Asian nations, with Singapore, Myanmar and Laos the exceptions.
Diplomatic influence also fell in nearly every country covered by the index.
Countries also struggled to navigate US tariffs, rising tensions in the South China Sea and ongoing competition between the United States and China.

Indonesia recorded the region's steepest decline in diplomatic influence, which the report attributed largely to President Prabowo Subianto's "haphazard approach to foreign policy". ( ABC News: Adam Kennedy )
Indonesia saw the greatest drop in diplomatic influence, a decline the report said largely reflected the country's "haphazard approach to foreign policy" under President Prabowo Subianto.
India rose to third place in the 2026 Asia Power Index, consolidating its position as a major power in the region.
In a year when most countries failed to gain diplomatic influence, India became more influential overall in Asia.
The country's Prime Minister Narendra Modi is now considered to be the second-most effective regional leader, behind Chinese President Xi Jinping.
"For the assessment of Modi's regional leadership, it's largely stability at a time of upheaval," Mr Sato said.
"A key factor we've found is continuity. Both Prime Minister Modi and External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar have established themselves in their roles."
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi was judged the second-most effective regional leader, behind Chinese President Xi Jinping, accroding to the report. ( Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein )
India has more political influence in the region now than when the index began eight years ago, although China's power remains 80 per cent higher than India's.
"India did struggle in 2026 with many internal challenges, which saw its scores for Economic Capability and Resilience decrease," Mr Sato said.
He also said the country's Diplomatic Influence score dipped slightly, "but by much less than others in the region".
"India has a very strong demographic and economic outlook, with, comfortably, the third-highest Future Resources score in the region."

items.title: Foreign minister to elevate AI as national security challenge
paras: Penny Wong says Australia will highlight AI risks in a major speech. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
Australia wants to shape the world order on AI and needs to move quickly in response to the rapidly emerging technology, Foreign Minister Penny Wong says.
It comes amid fears that the construction of AI data centres in Australia could be vulnerable to foreign actors.
The major foreign policy speech will be delivered in parliament on Tuesday.

Artificial intelligence will be elevated as a "major foreign policy and national security challenge" this week, with Foreign Minister Penny Wong warning that the emerging technology is giving foreign actors new tools to disrupt democracies.

Senator Wong will say that AI is transforming military power and reordering our lives and economies "in ways we cannot fully foresee" in a major foreign policy speech to be delivered to parliament on Tuesday.
"We have long known actors beyond our shores seek to interfere in Australia's democracy and in the lives of those who call Australia home," she will say.

She will refer to reports of disinformation, including an Iranian operation to use fake journalist personas to publish articles in a bid to sway opinion on the US-Iran conflict, and Russian covert operations to harness AI-generated deepfakes to influence US elections.
Senator Wong's speech comes amid warnings from Australia's spy chief about foreign interference in the construction of AI data centres.
ASIO director general Mike Burgess, in an interview with 60 Minutes, warned that foreign adversaries could seek some form of control over AI infrastructure covertly and "for nefarious reasons".
Mike Burgess says building AI data centres in Australia carries a foreign interference risk. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )
It also comes amid continued fallout over reports that Jensen Huang, head of powerful AI chip company Nvidia, was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy .
Mr Burgess's remarks follow US President Donald Trump warning of "tremendous" consequences for American tech companies building AI data centres overseas.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said there was a national security interest in building data centres in Australia, acknowledging Mr Burgess's remarks that with the AI boom came hype, opportunity and threat.
"Whenever you get that sort of capability onshore, it also becomes a magnet for people who would want to conduct foreign interference," Mr Burke told News24 on Sunday.
"So, we need to make sure that we are alert and that we are being very careful in the ownership structures that happen in Australia for data centres."
Senator Wong will say that Australia is strengthening critical technology and cyber resilience, as well as legislating mandatory AI safety standards.
Senator Wong will say that Australia cannot wait for international treaties and must move swiftly in the face of AI's rapid development.
"We must do what we can to ensure that the race to develop frontier AI, concentrated in a handful of companies and countries, does not reward speed over prudence," she will say.
"Australia is working with partners on AI safety, making it a shared, global endeavour."
She will say that Australia has helped to shape the international order on nuclear proliferation and by taking a lead in online safety.
The sentiments echo those made by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the UN in September, where he called for global cooperation on AI and argued for safety guardrails on the technology .
Over the weekend, Australia and China agreed to hold talks on AI , following Mr Albanese's visit to China for the APEC summit.
Senator Wong's speech, titled Securing Australia's future in a changing world, effectively replaces the concept of the foreign policy white paper.

In June, Senator Wong told Senate Estimates that such documents quickly become outdated, and she instead preferred to outline the government's foreign policy through major speeches and statements to parliament.

items.title: Bodies found, 36 workers missing after Indonesian factory fire
paras: A drone view of smoke rising from the fire-damaged PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory. ( Reuters: Stringer )
A fire has swept through a confectionary factory in Indonesia's Banten province, killing at least three workers and leaving 36 others unaccounted-for.
The fire broke out on Saturday evening at a confectionery factory in Cikande, in the Serang regency.
A fire has swept through a confectionary factory in Indonesia's Banten province, killing at least three workers and leaving 36 others unaccounted-for, officials say.
The blaze broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in the Serang district of Banten province, which borders the capital, Jakarta, at 5pm local time on Saturday.
Flames engulfed the three-story factory, sending thick black smoke into the sky, television reports showed.
Debris littered the floor of the burned-out structure, including twisted metal and blackened, corrugated iron roofing.
A company representative said on Sunday that 300 workers were inside when the blaze started.
Rescue workers seal a bag containing a victim's body following the factory fire. ( Reuters: Stringer )
The rescued included four injured workers, the National Search and Rescue Agency said in a statement.
The remains of the three killed were transferred to a hospital in seven black body bags for identification.

Authorities said the intensity of the fire had rendered the recovered victims unidentifiable via visual inspection, prompting efforts to collect DNA samples from relatives and personal belongings of the missing workers.
The cause of the fire was not immediately known. Survivors said the fire originated from a cooling unit on the third floor, local media reported.

Tubagus Mahfud, operations chief of the Serang fire department, said the blaze has been largely contained, but firefighters were still carrying out intensive cooling operations before they could access all parts of the factory.
A drone view of emergency services personnel gathered near body bags outside the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory. ( Reuters: Stringer )
He added that the remaining hotspots were concentrated in the central and rear sections of the building.
"We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control," Mr Mahfud said.
"Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously."
He also said the factory's production materials could cause the fire to reignite, making it critical to complete cooling operations.

Rizky Dwianto, an operations official at the Banten Search and Rescue Agency, said 15 fire trucks with water cannons were deployed to battle the flames in several parts of the facility more than 12 hours after the fire began.
A drone view shows flames engulf a factory at PT Fonusa Agung Mulia in Cikande. ( Reuters: Stringer )
A joint rescue team — including police, the military, the Indonesian Red Cross and volunteers — was at the scene.
"Authorities continue to coordinate with families and the company to determine the whereabouts of employees believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out," he said.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products.
It is part of Indonesia's United Family Food company, founded in 1981, according to its website.

It produces consumer goods across Indonesia, employs about 5,000 people and operates from its national headquarters and four international offices, serving a market of more than 250 million consumers.
Indonesia has experienced a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising concerns about workplace safety standards and emergency preparedness at manufacturing facilities.

items.title: Does the ICJ genocide ruling spell trouble for Israel?
paras: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) made history on Thursday as it ruled for the first time that a state had committed genocide. Myanmar was found to have both ‘committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State’ and to have ‘violated its obligations… to prevent genocide’. Experts are now considering what this verdict means for Israel, itself facing trial at the ICJ over its actions in the Gaza Strip.

The Myanmar verdict was the conclusion of a seven-year case brought by The Gambia and which featured eleven state interventions, including by the United Kingdom. While the case was already considered one of the most significant cases ever examined in international law, it took on even more significance after 2023 when South Africa referred Israel to the ICJ using the same mechanism. So, following this ruling, does it make it more likely that Israel will become the second state to be found guilty of genocide?
Several Israeli outlets recognised the implications for Israel’s Gaza case

The ICJ found that a ‘reasonable inference’ could be made that ‘Myanmar forces acted with genocidal intent’. The Court found that the Rohingya amounted to a distinct people, who faced large scale killings by security and state forces – organs of the state – and who faced acts of extreme violence. The Court found the number targeted was ‘significant’ and the Rohingya saw their rights ‘progressively eroded’ leaving them marginalised and vulnerable.

Speaking after the ruling, British barrister Philippe Sands, part of The Gambia’s legal team, stated that the judgment was an ‘extraordinarily thorough, rigorous, well documented, thoroughly assessed example of how evidence should be dealt with’, and he argued that the ICJ has stood up for the ‘rule of law’ at a time when international law is under attack.

Following Thursday’s ruling, Israeli outlets recognised the implications for Israel’s Gaza case. Israeli website Ynet quoted unnamed senior Israeli officials calling the ruling a ‘dangerous precedent’, as well as Tammy Caner of the Tel-Aviv based Institute for National Security Studies, who pointed out that the Myanmar judgment clarified that a military objective does not exclude genocidal intent. This implies that an Israeli defence predicated on actions taken in response to the October 7th attacks, however proportionality was judged, would not be enough.

Ahead of the ruling, legal experts explained to the Spectator that the case against Israel was seen as clearer than that of Myanmar. This is not to say that either would be found guilty, just that in their assessment there was stronger evidence and access when it came to the case against Israel.

This has been compounded by statements by Israel officials. One of the hardest issues when trying to judge genocide, is that of intent. Statements by Myanmar officials were considered. For example, Min Aung Hlaing – the current President of Myanmar – called it the ‘Bengali problem’ and an ‘unfinished job’. For Israel, there are several directly relevant examples. Several days after the October 7th attacks the Israeli defence minister Yoav Gallant referred to ‘no electricity, no food, no water, no fuel’ adding ‘we are fighting human animals’, while Israeli president Isaac Herzog apportioned blame to all Gazans saying, ‘it is an entire nation out there that is responsible’. By May 2025, finance minister Bezalel Smotrich was still asserting that Gaza would be ‘totally destroyed’. Some of these statements were used as evidence by a UN commission, which concluded they amounted to ‘direct and public incitement to commit genocide’. Israel vehemently rejects the genocide allegation.

In the Myanmar case, the ICJ ruled that a state should foresee that its actions could lead to one of genocide, even if one was not being perpetrated at the beginning of a conflict and thus should be reasonably expected to take preventative measures. This has clear implications for Israel – it means the Court, similarly, might accept that there were legitimate grounds for the response to the October 7th Hamas attacks but that Israel should have foreseen that the response could lead to, or increase the risk of, one of genocidal intent. In the case of Myanmar, the Court also found there had been historic prejudice and discrimination against the Rohingya people.

Legal experts had cautioned that the US may retaliate against the ICJ if a verdict of genocide was found. So far the US state department has greeted the result with caution and warned against ‘politicisation’ of the ICJ.

Many legal scholars point to the sanctions that the International Criminal Court (ICC) has faced from the US. The ICC – also based in The Hague – which prosecutes individuals not states, was originally targeted at the end of the first Trump administration. However, after Biden revoked sanctions, they were reinstated and ramped up during the second Trump administration, in response to the ICC’s actions against Israeli leaders. The ICC’s issuing of an arrest warrant against Netanyahu was itself criticised as ‘outrageous’ by the Biden administration.

Israel has benefitted historically from strong American bipartisan support for its actions, not just from the Trump administration, but this has changed dramatically since the October 7th attacks, evidence of which is seen not just in opinion polling but in the recent American midterms. The war with Iran, and support for Israel, was a major factor in the Democratic ‘tsunami’. A new generation of Democrats – including the first Muslim senator – have been elected, a group who certainly don’t demonstrate the same unconditional support for Israel.

In the last two years of the Trump presidency, it is now advantage Democrats and attention will turn to who their presidential nominee will be. One such contender is Georgia senator Jon Ossoff who, when asked if Israel was committing genocide, said it was ‘a question for the ICC. There is no doubt in my mind that Israeli forces prosecuting the war in Gaza violated the law of armed conflict’. He also dismissed his Republican opponent’s support for sanctions against the Court.

The ICJ may yet face retaliation from the Trump administration. For Israel, however, the midterms offered some evidence of how far American opinion has shifted. Less than three weeks later, the Court handed down its historic judgment on Myanmar. Israel’s final written submission is due in May 2029, with a judgment issued later that year or even into 2030, by which time Trump will have left office. Israeli governments have long banked on bipartisan support in Washington, but by the time the judges rule, Israel may find it has fewer friends there. In The Hague, the precedent set by the Myanmar judgment will still be there.

items.title: Reserve Bank issues Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) (Second Amendment) Regulations
paras: The Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 were superseded by the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, which were issued on January 13, 2026 , and became effective from October 01, 2026. The new regulations are principle based; intended to promote ease of doing business, especially for small exporters and importers; and empower Authorised Dealers to provide quicker and more efficient service to their customers. Based on subsequent feedback received from stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has issued Amendment Regulations to Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 that were notified on November 02, 2026 , and came into effect, retrospectively, from October 01, 2026 . In this regard, to facilitate better understanding of the new trade regulations by the exporters/importers and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank has placed a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026 on its website. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1531

items.title: RBI imposes monetary penalty on Fusion Finance Limited
paras: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 17, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹7.50 lakh (Rupees Seven Lakh Fifty Thousand only) on Fusion Finance Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of directions issued by RBI on ‘Know Your Customer (KYC)’ and ‘Internal Ombudsman’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under section 58G(1)(b) read with section 58B(5)(aa) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its financial position as on March 31, 2026. Based on the supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for failure to comply with the RBI directions. After considering the company's reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty: The company failed to obtain PAN or equivalent e-document thereof or Form 60 from customers, while establishing an account-based relationship with those customers; and, The company failed to escalate the partly or wholly rejected complaints to the Internal Ombudsman for a final decision within the prescribed time. This action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of this monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1537

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "High probability of meeting between PM Modi, President Xi": Former Indian envoy on patrolling agreement between India-C
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Gautam Bambawale , former India n Ambassador to China , Bhutan, and Pakistan said that the recent agreement on border patrolling between India and China along the Line of Actual Control ( LAC ) has opened up possibilities for a bilateral meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping in Kazan along the sidelines of the BRICS Summit and asserted that the probability of a meeting between the two leaders is "very high." He also noted that although India and China reached an agreement on patrolling arrangements ahead of the BRICS Summit in Kazan , Russia , this breakthrough is the result of discussions and negotiations between India and China , with no involvement from Russia . While speaking with ANI, Bambawale said, "On this question of the recent agreement on patrolling along the LAC , especially in eastern Ladakh, I do not think the Russia ns must have had a hand in it. It would have been discussions between India and China and negotiations between India and China that led to this agreement." He added, "Now that the problems on the border along the LAC have been sorted out, I think there is a very high probability that our Prime Minister Modi and the President of China , Xi Jinping , could have a bilateral meeting in Kazan . I think it would be a meeting to break the ice. I don't expect some great warmth suddenly. It will take time to rebuild the relationship from the setback that it had in the Summer of 2020. This situation has gone on for 4.5 years. So it will take some time to repair the relationship but I think this agreement will be a start and if there's a meeting between the two leaders at the summit level in Kazan on the sidelines of BRICS, then that will be another step towards restoring the relationship to what it was earlier." Bambawale further said that the agreement on patrolling arrangements implies that China is willing to restore the relationship between the two nations to its pre-2020 state, paving the way for progress in other sectors such as trade, commerce, and investment.

He said, "The agreement has come just before the BRICS summit takes place in the next few days in Kazan in Russia . I think what this implies is that the Chinese side is wanting to restore the relationship between India and China to what it was earlier. It wants the other aspects of the relationship like trade, commerce and investment to move ahead. It will of course take some time to restore the trust between the two countries. But at least I think a beginning can be made and perhaps there might be a meeting at the topmost level between PM Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping at Kazan ." The former India n Ambassador further noted that the agreement between India and China is expected to significantly boost the BRICS grouping, despite not necessarily indicating a closer relationship between India and Russia or China . "I won't say India is moving closer to Russia and China but I think the BRICS grouping will be immeasurably strengthened because of this understanding between India and China because of the cooling of tensions on the border between India and China and as India has always said that a peaceful border means that the rest of the relatrionship can also move ahead. So I believe that a better relationship between India and China will be better for the BRICS grouping," Bambawale told ANI. Bambawale further said, "If this implies that the status quo ante has been restored as it existed before the Chinese undertook the military action in eastern Ladakh in summer of 2020... then I think this is a very welcome development. The government of India should be congratulated on taking a firm position on this matter and that India 's stand has been vindicated after 4.5 years of face-to-face situation between India n and Chinese troops. If it means that the status quo ante has been restored, then we definitely welcome this agreement. It is a good agreement and we can move forward on the basis of this agreement." Notably, a day before, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who addressed a special media briefing ahead of PM Modi 's visit to Russia for the BRICS Summit , said India and China have reached an agreement on the patrolling arrangements along LAC . The agreement was reached ahead of the BRICS Summit which will be attended by PM Modi and Chinese President Xi. "On several areas along the Line of Actual Control , we held discussions with Chinese interlocutors, both on diplomatic as well as the military levels through meeting with military commanders at various levels. These discussions had in the past resulted in the resolution of standoffs at various locations. There are some locations and areas where stand-offs had not been resolved," said Misri. "Now, as a result of the discussions taking place over the last several weeks an agreement has been arrived at on patrolling arrangements along the LAC in the India - China border areas. This is leading to disengagement and eventually a resolution of the issues that had arisen in these areas in 2020," he added. (ANI)

items.title: Asia's Largest Mindfulness India Summit 2024 Marks a New Era for Corporate Culture and Personal Well-being with the Inau
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. Manish Behl, founder of the awards, explained, "Corporate success today goes beyond profit; it's about fostering environments where employees thrive mentally, emotionally, and physically. Our vision with these awards is to inspire a deeper integration of mindfulness in corporate cultures worldwide. By recognizing these pioneers, we hope these awards inspire companies and individuals to further integrate mindfulness into their environments, ultimately fostering happier, more productive workplaces, communities, and a more compassionate world." The awards were designed to acknowledge champions of mindfulness across categories, recognizing those who incorporate mindful practices to improve workplace culture, employee engagement, and societal impact. Winners ranged from corporate giants like Aditya Birla Group and Accenture to global educators and community leaders. items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
paras: lower demand GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff GLP-1 drugs could cut food demand enough to free farmland larger than Italy.

7 ... ... ... Credit: https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/wind-farms-and-agricultural-production-royalty-free-image/2183669700 Credit: https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/wind-farms-and-agricultural-production-royalty-free-image/2183669700 Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.

Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease,” blaming individual people for not having enough willpower . But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located, and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.

The UK government-commissioned national food strategy , finalized in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.

Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.

A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables, and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use, and the environment.

Rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.

GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.

The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production, and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.
Roslyn Henry is Lecturer, School of Biological Sciences, University of Aberdeen and Peter Alexander is Professor of Global Food Systems, University of Edinburgh .

items.title: November 22, 2015: The day Novak Djokovic won a record fourth straight ATP World Tour Finals in London
paras: Every day Tennis Majors looks back at the biggest moments in tennis history. On November 22, 2015, Novak Djokovic capped an exceptional season by clinching a record fourth consecutive Masters title

On this day, November 22, 2015, Novak Djokovic defeated Roger Federer in the final of the ATP World Tour Finals (6-3, 6-4). With this, the Serb, who had already set a record of 15 consecutive wins at the year-end tournament a few days earlier, became the first player in tennis history to triumph at this event more than three times in a row.

Novak Djokovic was born in 1987 in Belgrade. He entered the top 100 in 2005, finishing the year as world No 83. In 2006, he announced his arrival on the big stage by reaching the quarter-finals at Roland-Garros while being ranked only No 63, after he beat world No 9 Fernando Gonzalez in the second round.
items.impact: At the start of 2008, Djokovic triumphed for the first time in a Grand Slam tournament, edging Jo-Wilfried Tsonga in the Australian Open final (4-6, 6-4, 6-3, 7-6).

items.title: Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
